title: Building an AI Management Theory in Public

note.argument: The author begins by noting that clients value confidence over watching a thinker, highlighting the market pressure for certainty. Confronted with the emerging field of intelligent systems, they observe that implementations generate unexpected emergence and organisational knowledge that cannot be anticipated in advance. Because this knowledge only appears after deployment, large, upfront transformation programmes that assume a known destination are misguided. Instead, the author proposes an incremental, evidence‑driven redesign approach analogous to the Strangler Fig pattern, where each bounded capability is introduced, its governance implications observed, and the learning captured to shape the next step. Consequently, success metrics should shift from merely delivering capabilities to capturing the organisational knowledge produced. The overall argument is that public, transparent inquiry and a lens that reveals existing but hidden organisational dynamics are essential for leaders to navigate the co‑evolution of human and non‑human intelligence.
claims: Clients don’t generally pay to watch someone think; they pay for confidence.
Implementation of intelligent systems produces emergence that must be captured before it becomes organisational knowledge.
Large, upfront transformation programmes are trying to solve the wrong problem because the destination isn’t fully knowable until intelligent systems begin operating inside the organisation.
Organisations suffer from fragmented organisational learning because they fail to capture the knowledge generated by AI implementations.
Research should be done publicly, making reasoning visible, as a form of intellectual honesty rather than uncertainty.

title: The Real Lesson in AI Implementation

note.argument: The author begins by observing that many organisations prioritize technology choices—models, platforms, vendors—before addressing organisational factors, and when AI projects stumble they blame immature technology or poor adoption. However, a review of AI implementation guides reveals they devote far more attention to workflows, governance, ownership, and operating models than to model selection, indicating that the real difficulty lies in organisational design. Consequently, the primary constraint on AI adoption is not the technology but the organisation’s ability to absorb it. Implementation therefore should not be treated as a separate technical project; it is the process by which organisations discover the necessary redesign of decision‑making, authority, and work flows. Each deployment should yield both a functional AI capability and insight into how intelligent systems reshape work, making the central question shift from "how to implement AI" to "how intelligent systems change organisational design".
claims: We’re still putting the cart before the horse by starting with technology choices before organisational considerations.

The hard problems in AI projects are not selecting a model or writing a prompt but deciding who owns decisions, how work should flow, where authority sits, what controls are needed and how people and intelligent systems work together.
The primary constraint on AI adoption is the organisation trying to absorb it, not the technology itself.
Implementation is the mechanism through which organisations discover how they need to change.
Every AI deployment should leave the organisation with a working capability and a better understanding of how intelligent systems change the work around them.

title: The AI Operating Model Is Discovered, Not Designed

note.argument: Winter‑Tear begins by exposing the outdated management assumption that all operational intelligence is human, noting that AI now embeds intelligence in non‑human agents. This shift means the traditional, upfront design of an operating model—based on human‑centric structures, governance, and processes—is no longer sufficient. He argues that trying to answer every management question before any AI is deployed is a mistake; instead, organisations should launch a bounded, complete piece of work, observe how the AI interacts with real work, and let those observations reveal where decisions, ownership, and controls truly belong. Each deployment therefore yields both a functional capability and new organisational knowledge. By systematically capturing this evidence in learning loops, the accumulated knowledge becomes the operating model itself. Consequently, firms that iterate quickly, learning from each bounded deployment, will out‑perform those that spend years designing a perfect model in advance.
claims: The operating model isn’t something you fully design upfront and then implement; it’s something you discover through implementation.
Every AI implementation should produce two outputs: a working capability and organisational knowledge.
The mistake is assuming that all management questions about AI can be answered before implementation begins.
AI changes what management is organising because operational intelligence is no longer exclusively human.
Organizations should start with a bounded, complete piece of work rather than redesign the entire enterprise before learning.

title: The Operating Model Is the Real AI Harness

note.argument: The author begins by noting that early AI discussions focused on the model itself, then shifted to the harness as the source of capability. Observing that identical models and similar harnesses still yield divergent results, the author argues that the missing factor is the operating model of the organisation, which each harness inherits. Consequently, the capability of a harness emerges from that operating model, making organisational design the true determinant of AI success. The author rejects the view that improving the harness alone will solve performance gaps and instead proposes that designing intelligent systems is essentially the same as designing the organisation’s operating model, shifting strategic focus from model or harness selection to organisational design.
claims: Every harness inherits the operating model it is built to serve.
The harness is where the operating model becomes software.
The capability of the harness itself emerges from the operating model of the organisation in which it is deployed.
Designing intelligent systems and designing organisations are becoming the same problem.
Two organisations can make identical technology decisions and still experience radically different outcomes because the technology is inheriting two completely different operating models.

title: How Intelligent Systems Change the Design of Organisations

note.argument: The author begins by noting that for over a century organisations have been built on the assumption that intelligence resides in people, which has produced structures like departments, hierarchies, meetings and approvals to compensate for human cognitive limits. He observes that current AI discourse focuses on the capabilities of models and tools, while neglecting how these intelligent systems alter the underlying assumptions of organisational design. By pointing out that AI makes context retrieval cheaper, knowledge persistent, routine judgement delegable, and coordination less costly, he argues that the structures built to manage human limitations should be re‑examined. Consequently, management is not rendered obsolete but must evolve because the thing it organizes—intelligence—has fundamentally changed. The author concludes that the crucial question for the coming decade is not which models are best, but who can best understand and redesign organisations to accommodate distributed, machine‑augmented intelligence.
claims: For more than a century we’ve been designing organisations around a simple assumption that intelligence lives inside people.
Most conversations about AI still focus on the technology itself, but the more important question is how intelligent systems change the design of organisations.

If context becomes dramatically cheaper to retrieve, knowledge becomes persistent rather than personal, routine judgement can be delegated, and coordination costs fall, then the organisational structures built around those constraints deserve to be questioned.
Management has always been the discipline of organising intelligence.
Intelligent systems don’t invalidate existing management ideas; they change the conditions that gave rise to them.

title: The Great AI Reversal

note.argument: The author begins by noting a rapid reversal in management thinking, observing that early enthusiasm focused on ever‑improving AI models as the primary driver of transformation. Over the past two years, however, numerous failed pilots and unmet ROI have exposed a deeper problem: organisational dysfunction. The author argues that AI does not hide these flaws but makes them more visible, shifting the explanation for success and failure from the technology itself to the way organisations are designed, governed, and operated. Consequently, the next phase of AI impact will not come from new model releases but from organisations learning to redesign workflows, decision‑making, and governance so they can absorb AI capabilities. The reversal, therefore, is not technological but diagnostic, moving the locus of change from AI models to organisational capability.
claims: We have just experienced one of the fastest reversals in management thinking.
The difference isn’t the AI itself; it’s the organisation around it.
Organisations must transform themselves before increasingly capable AI can deliver the outcomes everyone was expecting.
Many AI pilots have failed to scale, promised ROI never materialised, and demonstrations collapsed in real businesses.
The explanation for AI outcomes has shifted from the model to the organisation.

title: From AI Activity to Operating Leverage

note.argument: The author begins by defining an AI operating model as the environment that converts AI capability into business value. He argues that AI alone does not generate value; value emerges only when the surrounding work can absorb the AI output. The main obstacle, he says, is a bottleneck where AI shifts rather than eliminates work, moving effort into judgement, routing, and exception handling. To overcome this, he proposes a non‑bureaucratic operating model that creates conditions for faster, safer learning. The reasoning proceeds through a series of steps: first, anchor AI to a concrete business lever; second, map the real work where AI will intervene; third, set delegation boundaries and authority levels; fourth, design interruption and evidence mechanisms within the workflow; and finally, measure success by outcomes rather than activity. By piloting small, stoppable, value‑focused workflows, organisations can develop reusable patterns that embed AI into their processes, leading to faster learning under control and true operating leverage.
claims: An AI operating model is the working environment that turns AI capability into value.
AI does not create value simply by being available; it creates value when the surrounding work is ready to absorb it.
The bottleneck is that AI rarely removes work cleanly; more often it merely moves the work to new judgement and routing steps.
An operating model is not a set of bureaucratic gates but the set of conditions that allow faster, safer learning.
AI must be attached to a business lever before the organisation multiplies use cases; otherwise it is not operating leverage.

title: Banks, Private Equity and AI Have No Time to Waste

note.argument: The author begins by observing that recent bank AI announcements are not mere hype because regulatory constraints force concrete governance, evidence, and explainability whenever AI touches critical functions. He extends this observation to private‑equity, noting that capital pressures compel firms to demonstrate measurable value from AI throughout the investment cycle. From these premises he concludes that banks and PE serve as litmus tests for genuine AI adoption. He argues that true AI value arises not from visible adoption or flashy demos but from measurable state changes that improve margin, working capital, pricing, forecasting, and other levers tied to the P&L. Consequently, AI should be embedded within the value‑creation plan, guided by strong strategy, talent, and governance that focus on high‑impact areas. The overall thrust is that AI must transition from an access narrative to an operating‑leverage discipline, and only organizations under regulatory or capital pressure can validate that shift.
claims: When AI touches regulated banking functions, the focus shifts from access to what the AI is allowed to do, who owns the decision, evidence, value moved, risk changed, and post‑fact explainability.
Private‑equity firms are forced by capital to prove AI creates measurable value throughout the investment lifecycle.
Value is created when a business changes in ways that can be measured, defended and carried through to the P&L, not by the appearance of AI activity.
AI should be part of the value‑creation plan itself, not a separate technology theme.
Banks and private‑equity firms are superior tests of serious AI adoption because they cannot hide behind hype.

title: The AI Mandate Problem

note.argument: The author begins by observing that many organisations have proliferating AI activities but lack a strong, explicit mandate to turn those activities into disciplined change. This missing authority causes AI work to stall, because no one is empowered to decide what AI should actually alter. The common starting point of asking "where can we use AI?" is too broad; instead, the author argues for framing AI projects around concrete, valuable, bounded business problems that the organisation is prepared to redesign around. Efficiency‑oriented AI fits existing structures and is therefore easier to mandate, whereas growth‑oriented AI cuts across functions and requires a clearer decision framework. The role of a Chief AI Officer (CAIO) is often misunderstood; its true value lies in integrating technical capability with decision authority, not merely coordinating pilots. A robust AI mandate must spell out AI’s purpose, the type of value sought, acceptable risk, who can approve actions, what evidence is needed, and who owns outcomes. Without such a mandate, AI initiatives drift among functions, leading to costly pilots without transformation. Ultimately, the author contends that access and usage alone are insufficient; real value emerges only when AI is embedded in measurable, governed, and scalable work, and that AI exposes any vagueness in decision‑making, making a clear mandate essential before scaling.
claims: Many organisations have AI activity but lack a mandate strong enough to turn that activity into disciplined organisational change.
Before an organisation can absorb AI well, someone must be authorised to decide what AI should change.
The right starting question is a real, valuable, bounded, and important business problem that the organisation is willing to change surrounding work for, not merely “where can we use AI?”.
If the organisation is not willing to change the surrounding work, AI initiatives remain limited to individual speed gains and do not become serious operating value.
Efficiency‑focused AI projects are easier to mandate because they fit existing structures, whereas growth‑focused AI projects are harder because they cut across many functions.

title: Banks Are Showing Us What Serious AI Adoption Actually Looks Like

note.argument: The author begins by noting that banks have the resources and regulatory pressure to apply AI, but argues that serious AI adoption is not merely about giving people access to tools. Instead, it requires embedding AI into core, high‑friction workflows—fraud, KYC, credit, etc.—so that measurable productivity gains, lower error rates, and auditable outcomes are achieved. Using Santander and Lloyds as concrete examples, the author shows that the shape of AI value claims (production automation agents, quantified speed and error improvements) matters more than the raw monetary figures, which can be opaque. The piece then stresses that in regulated banking, "agentic" AI must be tightly constrained, with human oversight, audit trails, and clear authority limits. This leads to the broader point that AI must become part of the operating system, not just a productivity add‑on, and that concerns about sovereignty and infrastructure (as illustrated by the Lumen Sovereign initiative) reflect a shift from tool access to control over critical AI capabilities. The overall reasoning moves from a description of superficial AI adoption, through evidence of deeper operational integration, to a call for governance, control, and infrastructure considerations as the final stage of serious AI adoption.
claims: Serious AI adoption looks like AI being absorbed into the operating fabric of the institution rather than sprinkling tools across an organisation.

Santander says it has more than 280 process‑automation agents in production across credit, fraud, KYC and operations, with card‑fraud claims in Brazil 95 % faster, up to 90 % automated and under 1 % error.
“Value from AI” is not a clean category unless you know exactly what is being counted.
Access is not the same as value; usage is not the same as transformation.
AI does not become strategically important because everyone can open a tool; it becomes important when attached to work that can be measured, governed, improved and scaled.

title: Satya Nadella Has Seen That the Frontier Model Story Is Becoming Untenable

note.argument: The author begins by observing that the hype around ever‑larger frontier models is becoming commercially, politically, and strategically unstable. While raw model capability still matters, it alone cannot drive the next wave of enterprise AI investment. Therefore, the defensible competitive edge shifts to the enterprise learning loop that surrounds a model—agents, workflows, private evaluations, governance, and institutional memory. Nadella’s piece, the author argues, warns that model advantage is fleeting; firms that can swap models without losing their own veteran expertise will find the learning layer more valuable. This creates a "sovereignty test" for organizations. Because all firms will eventually have access to comparable general‑purpose intelligence, advantage must move from the model itself to the loop that captures and compounds human and token capital. The author further contends that Microsoft has a vested interest in protecting its role as the control plane for that loop, since a future where value concentrates in a few frontier‑model labs would make Microsoft dependent and invite regulatory backlash. Consequently, Microsoft’s strategy should focus on owning the enterprise AI operating layer—cloud, identity, security, workflow integration—rather than winning the model race. The ultimate claim is that the next competitive battle will be over who can manage cost, routing, governance, and value‑per‑token at scale, not who has the smartest model.
claims: The frontier model story is becoming unstable commercially, politically, and strategically.
Raw model capability alone will not be enough to justify the next phase of enterprise AI spend.
The defensible layer is the enterprise learning loop around the model – agents, workflows, private evals, traces, governance, identity, data, security, and institutional memory.
Companies should not just rent intelligence from a frontier model; they need to build a cognitive loop between human capital and token capital.
Model advantage may become less durable, so organizations that can switch models without losing veteran expertise will find the learning layer more valuable.

title: The Web Is Slipping Away from Us

note.argument: The author begins by noting that the Web was originally designed for human visitors, with every layer—from the access model to the economic and content models—built around human attention. He then points to recent data showing that automated, agentic AI traffic now exceeds human traffic, and argues that these agents behave fundamentally differently: they treat the Web as infrastructure to be queried and invoked rather than a place to browse. This shift undermines the traditional commercial bargain that relied on human‑generated signals such as pageviews, clicks, and ad impressions. As a result, the familiar human encounter (visits, comments, citations) is being abstracted away, leaving value captured by agents without rewarding the original publishers. The turn in the reasoning is the recognition that the Web’s core assumption—human primacy—is being violated across multiple layers, which forces a re‑thinking of architecture, economics, and strategy. The conclusion is that success now depends on being legible and selectable to agents rather than merely visible to humans.
claims: The current Web was built for humans and assumed human visitors, shaping its entire attention‑based architecture.
The Web’s assumption of human visitors shaped almost everything around attention, from pages to ads to analytics.
Agents treat the Web less like a place to visit and more like infrastructure to interrogate, invoke, and move through.
Agents disturb the Web’s commercial bargain because they can consume value without producing the same attention‑based signals.
The traditional human encounter on the Web is being abstracted; a system can read your work so another person does not have to.

title: AI-Native Development Is a Management Test

note.argument: The author begins by observing that AI‑native development removes the traditional cost‑and‑time filter that historically forced organisations to justify software ideas, thereby accelerating production. This shift does not eliminate bottlenecks; it merely moves them from coding to requirements, prioritisation, governance, and adoption. Because the old production constraint no longer provides selection pressure, the author argues that management must redesign end‑to‑end workflows, embed the right contextual information in AI agents, and overhaul governance, measurement, and decision‑making processes. Without such systemic change, faster coding and testing are merely local accelerations that increase software volume without improving judgement, leading to over‑production and confusion. Consequently, the key challenge for leaders is to align the newfound speed with equally rapid improvements in organisational learning and decision quality; otherwise the danger is an abundance of poorly justified software rather than a shortage of it.
claims: AI‑native development is a new way for an organisation to learn.
AI‑native development can dramatically shrink the dead space between intent, build, test, and learning.
The bottleneck does not disappear when AI is introduced; it moves to other parts of the process.
Understanding where the bottleneck moves will be a defining management challenge of the next decade.
Real value from AI‑native development comes from end‑to‑end transformation of workflows, teams, and measurement, not just scattering agents across tasks.

title: When AI Enters the World, the World Changes

note.argument: The author begins by asserting that AI does not enter a static, inert setting but a complex, adaptive sociotechnical environment that reacts to new technologies. Because AI changes that environment, its impact goes far beyond raw model performance, reshaping coordination, trust, skills, and institutional incentives. This undermines the "solipsistic" view that treats the world as a fixed backdrop for prediction. The author illustrates how interdependent dynamics can produce counter‑productive outcomes (e.g., reservation‑system overbooking, radiology skill erosion). Consequently, decision‑makers should evaluate not only whether an AI works but also what new operating environment it creates, what behaviours it rewards, and how it alters human agency. The central turn is from a performance‑centric lens to an environment‑centric lens, arguing that real risk and value lie in the systemic changes AI provokes.
claims: AI does not just enter an operating environment; it changes the operating environment.
If AI changes the operating environment, the opportunity is much bigger than the model’s performance alone.
A powerful AI system does not pass through an organisation without leaving marks.
Even a very capable AI system can be poorly suited to the real world if interdependence is treated as scenery.
Boards and executives should ask what operating environment will form around an AI system, not just whether it performs well.

title: The Next AI Frontier Is Relief

note.argument: The author begins by critiquing the early AI focus on benchmark scores and model comparisons, arguing that this emphasis looked in the wrong place. He then turns to a new premise: AI’s value lies in situated intelligence—being embedded in real workflows, devices, and processes where its output can affect subsequent actions. From this premise he rejects the notion that model capability alone is sufficient, pointing to the shift from surprise‑driven excitement to transformation‑driven design. He highlights concrete challenges (state, verification, long‑horizon coordination) as opportunities for better products, orchestration, and human‑AI collaboration, and expands the scope to document intelligence, budget‑aware agents, and modular system architecture. By illustrating successful applications such as conservation technology, he shows how AI can relieve trapped capacity rather than merely automate tasks. The turn in his reasoning is the claim that the next AI frontier is not about chasing ever larger models but about integrating intelligence into operating models that respect constraints, budgets, and evidence. He concludes that organizations that master this integration will win, while those that chase spectacle will fall behind.
claims: AI is beginning to move out of the demo space and into the shape of real work.
The frontier is shifting from isolated intelligence to situated intelligence.

AI becomes useful when it has somewhere to stand inside a workflow, device, document, field site, scientific loop, financial process, customer journey, or operating model where its output can actually change what happens next.
The field is growing up from “can it sound right?” to “can it participate usefully in the system?”.

If agents struggle with state, verification, long‑horizon coordination, and structured execution, those are the places where better products, operating models, orchestration, and human‑AI collaboration can create value.

title: The Agent Pilot Was the Easy Part

note.argument: The author begins by noting that pilots only prove an agent can perform a task, not that the organisation is ready to embed that action in real workflows. Production, unlike a pilot, requires the business to have redesigned responsibility, authority, and evidence flows around the agent’s output. Because rule‑following does not guarantee correct outcomes, merely adding a human somewhere in the loop is insufficient; the human must occupy a genuine ownership point with the power to intervene before consequences occur. Therefore, before rolling out an agent, organisations must define an authority model, decide which actions need approval, ensure evidence travels with hand‑offs, and establish clear stop‑points for uncertainty. If these questions remain unanswered, the pilot has not shown production readiness. Only when the business can absorb the agent’s actions—by having the right governance and ownership structures—can the agent move from impressive experiments to dependable, scalable automation.
claims: The agent pilot was never the hard part.
Many agent projects break in production because the organisation has not redesigned responsibility, evidence, and authority around the agent’s task.
Rule‑following by an agent does not constitute ownership of the outcome.
“Human in the loop” is a weak solution unless the human is placed at a meaningful ownership point before consequences occur.
When agents move to production, the human role must shift from manual execution to designed judgement.

title: AI Does Not Remove Judgement. It Relocates It.

note.argument: The author begins by rejecting the common focus on merely keeping humans "in the loop" and argues that the crucial issue is the location of judgement within organisational work. They claim that AI does not eliminate judgement but shifts it from low‑value drafting and information‑gathering tasks to higher‑level decisions about truth, fairness, relevance, and consequence. This relocation changes the moral and economic geography of work, requiring new structures of authority, accountability, and supervision. Organisations that treat early AI pilots as evidence of having solved the problem miss the deeper question of where judgement now resides, leading to invisible responsibility, wasted review work, and disappointing ROI. The author therefore urges a systematic redesign of workflows to explicitly assign bounded authority and auditability to humans, so that AI can free judgement from the wrong places and place it where it adds real value.
claims: The real question is where judgement now lives.
It moves judgement from finding information to understanding what the information means in context.
It moves judgement from writing analysis to deciding what evidence deserves confidence.

It moves judgement from doing the task to owning the consequence when that task enters a customer process, a board paper, a legal argument, a clinical pathway, a financial forecast, or an operational workflow.
The person who once produced the thing may now be asked to judge the thing, govern the thing, explain the thing, challenge the thing, or decide whether the thing is ready to move.

title: AI Usage Is Not AI Value: A Maturity Model for Measuring What Actually Matters

note.argument: The author observes that many organisations equate AI usage metrics—seats deployed, tokens consumed, prompts written—with AI value, a conflation he labels Goodhart’s Law for AI. He argues that while usage metrics are useful in the early adoption phase to prove access and experimentation, they do not indicate whether AI actually improves work or business outcomes. Consequently, he proposes a maturity model of increasingly sophisticated KPIs—access, usage, adoption, workflow change, outcome evidence, cost‑per‑outcome, and governed scale—through which organisations must progress to demonstrate real value. By moving beyond enthusiasm metrics to proof standards that capture workflow transformation, economic impact, and safe scaling, leaders can make informed capital‑allocation decisions and avoid scaling ineffective pilots. The conclusion is that AI usage is a necessary starting point but a bad place to stop.
claims: AI usage does not equal AI value.
Serious AI adoption needs proof standards, not enthusiasm metrics.
The mistake is treating usage as value.
In the early phase, usage metrics are often necessary.
The upside of AI is real.

title: AI Needs Translators With Operating Authority

note.argument: The author begins by noting that the prevailing view of AI translators as mere communicators is too narrow. Drawing on BCG survey data that reveals a tension between CEOs seeking realism and boards demanding vision, and on observations that AI adoption outpaces organizational redesign, the author argues that without a role empowered to make operating decisions, AI initiatives suffer from fragmented accountability and fail to translate capability into business impact. The piece critiques the idea of a symbolic chief AI officer and instead proposes a translator with genuine operating authority who can bridge ambition and workflow reality, set proof standards, manage costs, and align governance with execution. By granting this authority, organizations can convert AI potential into funded, governed, and scalable outcomes, avoiding the pitfalls of hype, siloed responsibility, and ineffective governance.
claims: AI needs translators with operating authority.
The useful translator says, “If this system enters this workflow, here is what changes: decisions, costs, risks, support needs, controls, and the proof required before authority widens.”
Every serious organisation needs the capacity the title is trying, often clumsily, to describe.
If no one holds dedicated AI leadership capacity, the organisation ends up with distributed involvement but fragmented accountability.
Treating AI as the property of one function makes the organisation see clearly in one direction and partially everywhere else.

title: The AI Absorption Problem

note.argument: The author begins by observing that employees are already using AI faster than the surrounding organisational systems can keep up, creating a gap between individual capability and organisational readiness. This gap, termed the "AI absorption problem," is presented as the core issue, not merely a matter of adoption or deployment. The author defines three stages—adoption, deployment, and absorption—and argues that while many firms can adopt and deploy AI, they fail to absorb its effects because they have not redesigned incentives, decision rights, governance, and other institutional structures. The argument proceeds by showing that accelerating one part of a sociotechnical system merely shifts bottlenecks downstream, leading to hidden costs and limited value. Evidence from Microsoft, Stanford, and Anthropic reports is cited to illustrate that successful AI outcomes depend on process redesign, change management, and learning loops rather than model power. The author concludes that the true differentiator is an organisation's absorption capacity: its ability to capture, codify, and scale the learning generated by AI experiments. Consequently, leaders should shift focus from usage metrics to absorption questions that assess changed work, governance, risk, and evidence of scalable impact.
claims: People are moving faster than the systems around them.
The harder question is whether the organisation can absorb what AI changes once capability starts moving through real work.
Adoption asks whether people are using AI, deployment asks whether AI has entered the workflow, and absorption asks whether the organisation can carry the consequences.
AI can expand individual agency while exposing institutional immaturity.
Speeding up one part of the system does not automatically improve the system; it simply pushes more output into the next bottleneck.

title: When the Agent Market Finally Finds Its Word

note.argument: The author begins by observing that the AI market has long marketed agents with buzzwords like autonomy and intelligence, but this framing ignores the fact that a model alone never constituted a complete system. The introduction of the term “harness” signals a shift: the focus moves from the agent’s capabilities to the surrounding operating environment that must govern delegated action. By arguing that the model is only one component of a larger economic, organisational, and risk‑bearing system, the author shows that once agents can act, the problem becomes one of authority, not just functionality. The language of autonomy is therefore insufficient because it does not address legitimacy, permissions, identity, cost, memory, or retrieval. The author proposes that a “harness” – a layer of governance that enforces checks, logs evidence, manages cost, controls memory, and can revoke authority – is the missing piece. Drawing on how humans allocate authority, the author concludes that the critical question is not how autonomous an agent is, but what authority it has been granted and what conditions must hold for that authority to remain valid. The argument culminates in the claim that the model is not the operating unit; the governed workflow is, and only a robust harness can make the difference between competent‑looking and legitimate action.
claims: “Harness” is not just new agentic AI terminology; it signals that model capability was never the whole system.
Agentic AI is becoming useful not by making models smarter but by building the machinery around delegated action.
The word “harness” marks a shift from fascination with the agent to concern with the operating environment.
The model is not the whole economic, organisational, or risk‑bearing object; the real system includes what the agent can touch, infer, remember, cost, break, prove, and who can stop it.
Once a system can act, tool use stops being a feature demonstration and becomes an authority problem.

title: When Building Stops Being the Bottleneck

note.argument: The author begins by noting that traditional product systems treated building as the primary bottleneck, which justified extensive roadmaps, backlogs, and prioritisation rituals. With AI, building becomes faster and cheaper, weakening those constraints, but the need for choice remains and shifts to other parts of the process. The author warns that collapsing the gap between request and build can increase responsiveness without improving judgement, because fast prototyping cannot replace the reflective work that writing provides. Consequently, the new risk is a subtle feature‑factory where speed masks incoherence; companies may act on every customer signal without disciplined interpretation. The argument proceeds to claim that AI does not eliminate constraints but moves them to interpretation, coherence, and evidence discipline. Therefore, mature product leadership—focused on judgement, evidence evaluation, and maintaining product coherence—becomes more crucial, even as traditional PM rituals fade. The conclusion is that the product function persists, now more exposed, and must adapt to the new bottleneck of interpretation rather than capacity.
claims: When building gets faster and cheaper, those old constraints weaken, but choice does not disappear and instead moves elsewhere.
AI‑native companies are right to eliminate a lot of the wasteful product processes that existed when building was scarce.
When the gap between request and build collapses, a company can become much more responsive without becoming much wiser.
AI does not remove constraints; it moves them to interpretation, coherence, supervision, and learning quality.
Speed does not automatically become learning.

title: Most Organisations Are Looking for AI Value in the Wrong Layer of Work

note.argument: The author begins by observing that many organisations have plenty of AI activity but see little business impact because they focus on surface‑level tasks that merely accelerate existing work. This leads to the introduction of the "mapping problem" – the difficulty of locating where AI can truly affect production constraints. Evidence from an INSEAD field experiment shows that firms whose leaders were helped to re‑map their work (search quality) discovered more use cases and achieved higher revenue and lower capital demand, indicating that value comes from reorganising production, not just providing tools. The author argues that task acceleration without changing the underlying constraint merely feeds the same bottleneck, yielding no strategic improvement. Consequently, organisations must shift from compiling use‑case inventories to mapping and redesigning the deeper constraints in their workflows, especially as scale adds complexity. The scarce capability is the ability to perform this mapping, not merely access to AI technology.
claims: Most organisations are not struggling to find AI use cases; they are struggling because the use cases they find are too close to the visible surface of work.
Usefulness is being hunted in the wrong layer.
The “mapping problem” describes the difficulty of discovering where and how AI creates value within an organisation’s production process.
Access was not the differentiator; search quality was.
Surface‑level AI tasks may save time but are often too close to the surface to change the business.
